title: Strict-local description and base-change criterion for oriented nearby cycles
statement:
Let $\Lambda$ be a commutative ring annihilated by $m\geq1$, and $f:X\to Y$ a morphism locally of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Use $V_f$, $R\Psi_f$, the ordinary comparisons and $\Psi$-goodness of [def-trf-oriented-nearby-cycles]. For a geometric point $x$ of $X$ [def-weil-geometric-point] with image $y$, put $X_{(x)}$ and $Y_{(y)}$ for the strict localizations [def-weil-pbc-strict-henselization-limit], $g=f_{(x)}:X_{(x)}\to Y_{(y)}$, and $K_{(x)}=K|_{X_{(x)}}$ for $K\in D(X_{\mathrm{Et}},\Lambda)$. There is a canonical morphism $\sigma_x:(Y_{(y)})_{\mathrm{Et}}\to V_f$ sending a geometric generization $t\to y$ to the vanishing-topos point $(x,y\leftarrow t)$. The inverse images $\sigma_x^*$ are exact and preserve derived tensor, are jointly conservative on $D(V_f,\Lambda)$, and have canonical natural isomorphisms
$$\sigma_x^*R\Psi_fK\simeq Rg_*K_{(x)}.$$
These identifications take ordinary comparisons to ordinary strict-local direct-image comparison maps and lax tensor maps to the tensor maps adjoint to the tensor of direct-image counits. In particular they identify the restriction of the specified oriented external-product comparison with the direct-image external-product comparison on the strict localizations of the two factors and their product.

Moreover, $(f,K)$ is $\Psi$-good if and only if, for every $x$, $Rg_*K_{(x)}$ commutes with localized base change: for every commutative square $g h=k g'$ of local morphisms of strictly local schemes, with $k:Y'\to Y_{(y)}$, $h:X'\to X_{(x)}$, $g':X'\to Y'$ and $X'\to X_{(x)}\times_{Y_{(y)}}Y'$ a strict localization, the canonical map
$$k^*Rg_*K_{(x)}\longrightarrow Rg'_*h^*K_{(x)}$$
is an isomorphism. Here the comparison is the unique map whose adjunct under $g'^*\dashv Rg'_*$ is
$$g'^*k^*Rg_*K_{(x)}\simeq h^*g^*Rg_*K_{(x)}\xrightarrow{h^*\varepsilon_g}h^*K_{(x)},$$
where $\varepsilon_g$ is the direct-image counit; use the ordinary derived direct-image adjunctions of [def-kun-projection-formula-map]. A square with this strict-localization property is called essentially Cartesian. This localized base-change invariance holds again for every such $(g',h^*K_{(x)})$.

source.place: Remark A.2, equation (A.2.1) and (1), pp. 1--2; first paragraph of the proof of Theorem A.3, equation (A.3.1), p. 2. Construction of sigma: Illusie, Around the Thom--Sebastiani theorem, (1.11.1)--(1.11.6), (1.12.6), pp. 12--13, https://www.imo.universite-paris-saclay.fr/~luc.illusie/Illusie-nearby-cycles28.pdf; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Put $j:X_{(x)}\to X$ and $k:Y_{(y)}\to Y$. The closed geometric points of these strict localizations give $g:X_{(x)}\to Y_{(y)}$ as a local morphism. The local-projection lemma supplies the canonical section $\widetilde\sigma_x:(Y_{(y)})_{\mathrm{Et}}\to V_g$, built from the constant closed point $x\epsilon$ and the natural $2$-morphism $1\Rightarrow y\epsilon$. Let $v:V_g\to V_f$ be the morphism induced by $(j,k)$. Define $\sigma_x=v\widetilde\sigma_x$. The universal property shows that its geometric point at $t\to y$ is $(x,y\leftarrow t)$ and makes the construction canonical. In particular the specialization datum is the counit from the constant closed-point sheaf, rather than the identity arrow at $y$.

source.place: Illusie §§1.3, 1.11--1.12; Zheng Appendix A.1--A.2 and (A.3.1). Read online; no downloaded literature added.

proof.text: First suppose $K\in D^+(X_{\mathrm{Et}},\Lambda)$. Form the canonical comparison $v^*R\Psi_fK\to R\Psi_gj^*K$ from the definition. Pull back by $\widetilde\sigma_x$, then use $\widetilde\sigma_x^*\cong p_{2,*}$ from the local-projection lemma. Since $p_{2,*}$ is exact and $p_2\psi_g=g$, the resulting target is $Rg_*j^*K$: both are right adjoint to $g^*=\psi_g^*p_2^*$. This constructs a natural map $\alpha_K:\sigma_x^*R\Psi_fK\to Rg_*j^*K$. At a geometric point $t$ of $Y_{(y)}$, oriented-point cohomology (take the second scheme to be $Y$ and its map the identity) computes the source as $R\Gamma(X_{(x)}\times_{Y_{(y)}}Y_{(t)},K)$. The strict-local stalk formula computes the target as the same complex: $g$ is a morphism between affine schemes, hence qcqs, and the coefficients are torsion since $m\Lambda=0$. Their maps are the restrictions from the same pointed neighbourhoods. Thus $\alpha_K$ is an isomorphism by geometric-stalk conservativity. Apply the coefficient-forgetting theorem (use the identity base-change square for $g$): it identifies the bounded-below module direct image with the abelian one. Its exact inverse-image comparison identifies the restrictions as well, so the abelian strict-local stalk formula applies to our module complex. No unbounded version of either bounded-below formula is being used. Ind-etale invariance identifies the strict localization of $Y_{(y)}$ at $t$ with $Y_{(t)}$.

source.place: Illusie §§1.3, 1.11--1.12; Zheng Appendix A.1--A.2 and (A.3.1). Read online; no downloaded literature added.

proof.text: For arbitrary $K$, take a K-injective resolution $K\to I^\bullet$ with injective terms, using the resolution-existence node on a small representative of $X_{\mathrm{Et}}$. Apply step 2 to a single injective sheaf $J$. Since $R\Psi_fJ=\psi_{f,*}J[0]$, it shows that $j^*J$ is $g_*$-acyclic, and in degree zero gives the natural underived isomorphism $\sigma_x^*\psi_{f,*}J\cong g_*j^*J$. The universal-(*) node gives an integer $N$ with $R^qg_*F=0$ for all module sheaves $F$ and $q>N$; only the bound at this $x$ is needed. The finite-cd acyclic-complex theorem now says that the possibly unbounded complex $j^*I^\bullet$, all of whose terms are $g_*$-acyclic, computes $Rg_*j^*K$. Applying the degree-zero isomorphism termwise gives $\sigma_x^*\psi_{f,*}I^\bullet\cong g_*j^*I^\bullet$, which represents $\alpha_K$. Naturality of the acyclic-complex comparison shows that this is the same derived comparison, and proves the unbounded assertion without assuming that $j^*I^\bullet$ is K-injective.

source.place: Illusie §§1.3, 1.11--1.12; Zheng Appendix A.1--A.2 and (A.3.1). Read online; no downloaded literature added.

proof.text: Inverse image for a geometric morphism with constant coefficients is exact, by the nearby-cycle definition. Apply the derived tensor-pullback theorem to $\sigma_x$, with the coefficient-ring map the canonical isomorphism $\sigma_x^{-1}\Lambda\cong\Lambda$. It gives $\sigma_x^*(A\otimes^LB)\cong\sigma_x^*A\otimes^L\sigma_x^*B$ for arbitrary unbounded $A,B$.

source.place: Illusie §§1.3, 1.11--1.12; Zheng Appendix A.1--A.2 and (A.3.1). Read online; no downloaded literature added.

proof.text: Every specialization-triple point of $V_f$ has the form $(x,y\leftarrow t)$ for a geometric point $t$ of $Y_{(y)}$; the specialization is precisely its map into the strict localization. By the product-point conservativity node these point functors detect sheaf isomorphisms. They are exact, so for a derived morphism $a$ they commute with every cohomology sheaf of $\operatorname{Cone}(a)$. If every $\sigma_x^*a$ is invertible, all the triple stalks of all these cohomology sheaves vanish, hence the cone is zero. This proves joint conservativity on the unbounded derived category.

source.place: Illusie §§1.3, 1.11--1.12; Zheng Appendix A.1--A.2 and (A.3.1). Read online; no downloaded literature added.

proof.text: For a commutative local strict-local square $gh=kg'$, the universal property identifies $v\sigma_{x'}=\sigma_xk$ with the specified $2$-morphisms, because the constant closed-point counit is natural under a local map. Unfold the mate defining the ordinary nearby comparison, then the unit defining the local-projection isomorphism. After $\alpha$ its adjunct under $g'^*\dashv Rg'_*$ is exactly $g'^*k^*Rg_*K_{(x)}\cong h^*g^*Rg_*K_{(x)}\xrightarrow{h^*\varepsilon_g}h^*K_{(x)}$: the intervening unit followed by counit cancels by the adjunction triangle identity. This specifies the ordinary strict-local comparison, including for an essentially Cartesian square; no invertibility is needed for the identification.

source.place: Illusie §§1.3, 1.11--1.12; Zheng Appendix A.1--A.2 and (A.3.1). Read online; no downloaded literature added.

proof.text: For $A,B$, the local lax map is specified by the adjunct $g^*(Rg_*A\otimes^LRg_*B)\cong g^*Rg_*A\otimes^Lg^*Rg_*B\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_A\otimes^L\varepsilon_B}A\otimes^LB$. The defining adjunct of the oriented lax map becomes this composite by step 4 and the same triangle identities as step 6. For two factors and a point $x$ of their product, the projections give $x_i$ and the functorial maps $X_{(x)}\to X_{i,(x_i)}$. The oriented external-product map is, by definition, the tensor of the two ordinary comparisons followed by the lax map. Step 6 identifies each ordinary comparison and the present adjunct identifies its last map. Thus the whole composite becomes the direct-image external-product map on these strict localizations, even though their scheme product need not itself be strictly local.

source.place: Illusie §§1.3, 1.11--1.12; Zheng Appendix A.1--A.2 and (A.3.1). Read online; no downloaded literature added.

proof.text: Let $Y'\to Y$ be arbitrary and $T=X\times_YY'$. At a geometric point $x'$ of $T$, put $x$ for its image and localize the target at $y'=f'(x')$. Its functorial map $Y'_{(y')}\to Y_{(y)}$ is local. Put $Q=X_{(x)}\times_YY'_{(y')}$ and $W=X_{(x)}\times_{Y_{(y)}}Y'_{(y')}$. First, $Q\to T$ is the composite of the base changes of $X_{(x)}\to X$ and of $Y'_{(y')}\to Y'$, both ind-etale by their pointed-etale limit construction (on affine neighbourhoods); two applications of the ind-etale invariance node identify $T_{(x')}$ with the strict localization of $Q$ at the induced point $q$, which lies over the closed points of $X_{(x)}$, $Y'_{(y')}$ and $Y_{(y)}$. Second, $W=Q\times_ZY_{(y)}$ for $Z=Y_{(y)}\times_YY_{(y)}$ and the diagonal $Y_{(y)}\to Z$. On an affine neighbourhood $\operatorname{Spec}A$ of $y$, $Y_{(y)}=\operatorname{Spec}B$ with $B$ ind-etale over $A$, so the affine strict-local base-change node computes the strict localization of $Z$ at the diagonal closed point $z$ as $Y_{(y)}\times_{Y_{(y)}}Y_{(y)}$, using the closed-point-localization node for $S'_{(f'\bar x')}\cong S'\cong S_{(\bar u)}$ with $f=\mathrm{id}$; both projections being the functorial maps, the diagonal is the strict-localization map $Z_{(z)}\to Z$. Hence $W=Q\times_ZZ_{(z)}$, and the closed-point-localization node (base $Z$, point $z$; $q$ lies over the closed point) gives $W_{(q)}\cong Q_{(q)}\cong T_{(x')}$. So $T_{(x')}\to W$ is a strict localization and the square is essentially Cartesian. Consequently step 6 turns the restriction of the global comparison into one of the maps in the asserted local criterion. If all such maps are invertible, step 5 reflects invertibility of the global comparison. This proves the implication from the local criterion to $\Psi$-goodness.

source.place: Illusie §§1.3, 1.11--1.12; Zheng Appendix A.1--A.2 and (A.3.1). Read online; no downloaded literature added.

proof.text: Conversely take any essentially Cartesian square in the statement. Use the composite $Y'\to Y_{(y)}\to Y$ as a global base change and let $T=X\times_YY'$. The closed point of $X'$ defines a geometric point $x'$ of $T$. The argument of step 8 (with $Y'_{(y')}=Y'$) shows $X'\cong T_{(x')}$, compatibly with $h$, and $Y'$ is its own strict localization at its closed point. Therefore its displayed local comparison is step 6's restriction of that global comparison. If $(f,K)$ is $\Psi$-good it is invertible. For stability, a subsequent essentially Cartesian square over $(g',h^*K_{(x)})$ corresponds likewise to strict localizations of successive global base changes of $f$. The defining mates for successive comparisons compose: their adjunct is the composite of the two pulled-back counits, with the middle unit/counit cancelled. Thus $\Psi$-goodness survives global base change and the preceding local test applies again to $(g',h^*K_{(x)})$. This proves the stability clause as well as the converse.

tool_uses.why: Its ordinary unbounded direct-image adjunction and explicit counit specify the strict-local ordinary and tensor mates; the trace-formula unit supplies no separate definition of this adjunction.
Its pointed-etale inverse-limit construction identifies the schemes used in the strict-local tests; the trace-formula unit uses this general scheme construction.
Its unbounded acyclic-term comparison computes Rg_* on the restricted injective resolution using the finite bound; it is a general homological tool, not a replacement for specialization.
Its unbounded monoidal pullback isomorphism applies to each sigma_x with the constant coefficient-ring isomorphism; it supplies the general tensor comparison used by this unit.
Its conservative geometric-stalk family detects the bounded-below comparison on Y_(y) in the coefficient universe; it is a general etale-site tool.
It supplies a K-injective resolution with injective terms on a small representative site; the trace-formula definition uses this general resolution theorem.
Its D+ torsion stalk formula computes Rg_* at t for the affine, hence qcqs, map g; this general strict-local tool supplies the target calculation.

Its exact inverse-image and D+ direct-image coefficient comparisons justify applying the abelian torsion stalk formula to constant-Lambda modules; no trace-formula node supplies this general comparison.

Its clauses (1), (3) and (4) supply the local functorial maps of strict localizations and their compatibility with pointed neighbourhoods; this is a general scheme tool needed in the strict-local tests.

Steps 8-9: computes the strict localization of Y_(y) x_Y Y_(y) at the diagonal closed point (Y_(y) ind-etale over an affine neighbourhood), identifying the diagonal with a strict-localization map; a general scheme tool absent from the trace-formula unit.

Steps 8-9: strict localizations are unchanged by base change along a strict localization of the base at points over its closed point, and a strict localization is its own localization at the closed point; a general scheme tool absent from the trace-formula unit.
